Hinged Pythagoras 3

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: This is a picture to explore, not a game to win: two squares and two swinging triangles can be turned into a tilted square.
How to play: Drag the round point along the bottom of the left shape, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Move the turn slider, then press Turn to 90° or Reset.

0°
Look for the math

The applet is a droodle: "What is it?" It draws two copies of a staircase made from a small square of side a and a larger one of side b. Two right triangles are marked in each copy. Turn the right-hand pair a quarter turn and the outline becomes a tilted square. The pieces never stretch, so whatever the eye sees, their total space cannot change.

Two squares side by side

Point M sits on the bottom of the left staircase. The two lengths are a = M.x − L0.x and b = L1.x − M.x, so the whole bottom edge is a + b. The staircase is just a square of side b next to a square of side a: its area is a² + b². The marked triangles have legs a and b and sloping side c = √(a² + b²); their area is ab/2 each. The dashed line is the cut between the two squares.

What the quarter turn does

One triangle swings about the top corner of the b-square, the other about the top corner of the a-square, in opposite directions. A swing is a rigid move, so each triangle keeps its three sides and its area — an invariant. The two fixed lines from the hinges to the moving point also have length c. At exactly 90° the two free corners meet, and those four length-c lines enclose a square of side c and area c². Since the same four pieces fill the two smaller squares before the turn, c² = a² + b², the Pythagorean theorem. This is a hinged dissection. The logic test checked the square and the tiling for all 201 whole-pixel hinge positions at 90°, every angle from 0° to 90°, and every drawn point against a second reading of the applet's bytecode.

The original page and its siblings

The applet's own page, Pythagorean Theorem By Hinged Dissection I: What is it?, still embeds APPLET CODE="HingedPythagoras3" WIDTH=640 HEIGHT=460 and points to Proof #2. That proof says: start with squares of sides a and b side by side, draw two triangles with sides a, b, c, then rotate them 90° about their top vertices, one clockwise and one counterclockwise; "the resulting shape is a square with the side c and area c²." The test confirms that claim for every hinge position. It is a different dissection from Hinged Pythagoras (Proof #9: two equal squares cut into four triangles) and Hinged Pythagoras 2 (Proof #10: four triangles inside one square). The applet's info string says "Proof #36", which is another dissection by J. E. Böttcher; this port follows the page's Proof #2. Two harmless quirks are kept: the scrollbar is declared 0–95 but its thumb of 5 makes Java stop the value at 90, and at 90° the applet computes a maximum of two corners that it never uses.

Drag M close to one end: one triangle becomes very thin. Press Turn to 90° — the tilted square still has area a² + b².
